10580-the-positive-school-of-criminology:
Italian criminologist Enrico Ferri gave these three lectures at the University of Naples on April 22, 23, and 24, 1901, and Ernest Untermann's translation appeared in Chicago in 1908. Ferri speaks for the "positive" school of criminology, which studied crime as a fact of nature and society rather than as a free choice of the will alone.

The lectures argue that crime grows from a mix of personal traits, social conditions, and circumstance, and that punishment should fit the danger a person poses, not just the act done. Ferri urges prevention, reform, and scientific study over harsh revenge. Readers get a short, forceful statement of ideas that reshaped how courts and reformers thought about crime.
10665-life-letters-and-epicurean-philoso:
Ninon de l'Enclos, the celebrated beauty and wit of seventeenth-century Paris, is the subject of this 1903 volume of life, letters, and philosophy. Chapters follow her youth, her mother's death, her growing fame, her friendships, and her lovers, including the Villarceaux affair and the Marquis de Sevigne. Her letters to Sevigne and her exchange with Saint-Evremond are printed in full.

The book presents Ninon as a free mind who lived by pleasure, reason, and loyalty to friends, in the manner of Epicurus. It also paints the morals and manners of her age. Readers get a vivid portrait of a woman who defied convention and stayed famous into a remarkable old age.
10726-outlines-of-lessons-in-botany-part:
Jane H. Newell wrote Outlines of Lessons in Botany, Part I, From Seed to Leaf, in 1888 for teachers and for mothers studying with their children. Illustrated by H. P. Symmes, the book begins with plants and their uses for food, clothing, air, and fuel. It then guides young learners to raise seedlings in the schoolroom.

Lessons study morning-glory, sunflower, bean, and pea, compare roots such as carrot, onion, and potato, and examine buds of horsechestnut, magnolia, and lilac. Directions are practical and clear. Families and schools get a gentle, hands-on botany course, built on watching real plants grow.
11077-ebooks-neither-e-nor-books-paper-f:
Cory Doctorow delivered this paper at the O'Reilly Emerging Technologies Conference in San Diego on February 12, 2004, under the title Ebooks: Neither E, Nor Books. Doctorow had released two novels and most of a story collection online under a Creative Commons licence. He argues that ebooks then were neither good electronic texts nor good books.

Doctorow discusses piracy panic, writers using false names on ebook newsgroups for fear of retaliation, and mischievous book-rippers said to plant deliberate errors, a claim he doubts for lack of evidence. The talk, dedicated to the public domain, captures early ebook debates: access, copying, and authors' fears, before ereaders and phones changed the market.
11397-the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-i:
Volume three of Samuel Johnson's Works, in the 1825 nine-volume edition, contains the second volume of the Rambler, essays numbered 106 through 135 and beyond. Topics include the vanity of authors' expectations, Properantia's hopes of confusion, the misery of prostitutes, life well employed, the education of a fop. repentance, youth's haste, Hymenæus's courtship, punishments proportioned to crimes, the young trader turned gentleman, the narrowness of fame, and the dangers of imitating Spenser.

Johnson's Rambler essays, published twice weekly in the 1750s, made his reputation as a moralist. This volume shows his range: character sketches, literary criticism, and moral argument in balanced prose. Readers approaching Johnson will find the Rambler here in a standard collected form.
1149-from-london-to-land-s-end-and-two-l:
Daniel Defoe, author of Robinson Crusoe, rides from London to Land's End and writes what he sees. His subjects are towns, ports, mines, and markets, with notes on trade, roads, and the people who work them. The journey runs through the West Country in the early eighteenth century.

Defoe's eye is that of a merchant and a journalist: he counts ships, weighs wool, and judges inns. The letters add gossip and detail from the road. The book gives a lively, ground-level view of Georgian England, and it still serves historians and travelers alike.
11771-occasional-papers-selected-from-th:
R. W. Church's Occasional Papers, second volume, gathers pieces from the Guardian, the Times, and the Saturday Review between 1846 and 1890. Church, sometime rector of Whatley and Dean of St. Paul's, writes first on Gladstone and the royal supremacy, Joyce on spiritual courts, and Privy Council judgments.

Later papers take up the Purchas case, disendowment, Mozley's Bampton lectures, and Renan's Vie de Jésus, Les Apôtres, and Souvenirs d'enfance. Lives of Frederick Robertson, Baron Bunsen, and Bishop Wilberforce close the set. The volume is a churchman's criticism of his age, collected after his death.
12006-a-handbook-to-agra-and-the-taj-sik:
E. B. Havell's 1904 Handbook to Agra and the Taj, Sikandra, Fatehpur-Sikri, and the Neighbourhood guides visitors through Mughal India, opening with a historical introduction on the great Moguls. Chapters trace Babar's connection with Agra, Humayun and the interregnum of Sher Shah, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and his monuments, and Aurangzib.

Havell, an art historian, pairs history with description, so a traveller can move from the story of a ruler to the building he left behind. The handbook covers the Taj itself, Sikandra, and Fatehpur-Sikri, treating architecture as the record of a dynasty. It remains useful as a compact, scholarly companion to one of India's most visited regions.
12045-women-in-the-fine-arts-from-the-se:
Clara Erskine Clement's 1904 book Women in the Fine Arts, from the seventh century B.C. to the twentieth century A.D., opens with an Alinari photograph of Elisabetta Sirani's Infant Christ in the Bologna Gallery. Clement's prefatory note explains that she sent a circular to many artists in Great Britain, Europe, and the United States, asking where their work could be studied.

The book surveys women painters, sculptors, and illustrators across more than two thousand years, from ancient Greece to modern studios. Clement's survey was pioneering: it treated women artists as a continuous tradition, not as exceptions. It remains a useful guide to names and works that larger histories had overlooked.
12050-the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-i:
Volume 4 of Samuel Johnson's works, printed in 1825 as part of the nine-volume Oxford edition, gathers The Adventurer and The Idler. Its prefatory notice explains that The Adventurer was projected in 1752 by Dr. John Hawkesworth, partly from admiration of The Rambler, which had then ceased to appear.

Hawkesworth's style and sentiments, the notice says, evidently followed Johnson's example from the start, and Johnson himself contributed to the periodical. The volume preserves two of the great eighteenth-century essay series, in which short, moral. Literary pieces addressed readers week by week on manners, books, and human nature.
12455-legends-of-the-middle-ages-narrate:
H. A. Guerber's 1896 retelling gathers the legends that fed medieval literature and art, written to familiarise young students with them. Charlemagne and Roland, King Arthur, Tristan and Isolde, and other heroes of romance appear in plain narrative, each tale chosen for its place in later books, pictures and music.

Guerber links story to source, showing how a legend lived on in poetry, drama and painting after its first telling. The preface frames the book as a doorway, not a scholarly study: enough plot, character and wonder to let a reader meet the old tales and then follow them further. Its value lies in that map-making, joining many separate cycles into one readable whole.
12523-crusaders-of-new-france-a-chronicl:
William Bennett Munro's 1918 chronicle, in the Chronicles of America series, tells of crusaders of New France, the fleur-de-lis in the wilderness. Dedicated to Father Henri Beaudé, the book moves from France of the Bourbons and a voyageur of Brittany to the founding of New France. The age of Louis Quatorze and the iron governor follow.

La Salle and the voyageurs, the church, seigneurs, coureurs-de-bois, agriculture, industry, trade and daily life follow. Munro writes a clear, popular history of French Canada, fond of its missionaries, soldiers and traders. The volume offers a compact, readable account of a French empire in America, and of the people who carried its flag inland.
12807-dick-prescott-s-fourth-year-at-wes:
Dick Prescott's fourth year at West Point, in Hancock's companion volume to the Annapolis finale, moves toward shoulder straps. Dick reports a brother cadet, faces Jordan's revenge, and endures the cadet silence, a cold shoulder from his class. A class meeting, a baseball gait found late, and the Army-Navy game build to the close.

A quiet study scene, where Dick finds a report he should have turned in before supper formation, shows academy routine pressing on honour. Greg Holmes stands by through each trial. The book gives Dick's West Point years their graduation payoff, with sport, loyalty, and duty in balance.
13133-ten-reasons-proposed-to-his-advers:
Edmund Campion, a Jesuit priest, wrote his Ten Reasons in Latin as a challenge to dispute in the Oxford divinity schools. This edition gives the Latin text with an English translation, plus a preface on the work's long fame. Campion's tract passed through forty-seven editions across Europe, and the humanist Muret called it written by the finger of God.

The translator calls it no dry divinity, but a knight's trumpet call to come forth and argue. Its ten theses defend the Catholic faith against all comers, with citations from fathers and councils in the notes. The book is a landmark of Reformation debate, valued for its bold form as much as for its arguments.
1323-history-of-the-conquest-of-peru-wit:
William Hickling Prescott opens this history with a full view of Inca civilization: its roads, laws, religion, and arts, before Pizarro's ships appear. The narrative then follows the conquest itself, from Cajamarca's ambush to the wars among the Spaniards who divided the spoil.

Prescott's preliminary chapters give the Incas their due as builders and rulers, not mere victims, while his tale of the conquest keeps a novelist's pace. The history, a companion to his Mexico, remains a landmark of American scholarship. It draws readers who want the whole Peruvian story.
13614-studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-v:
The fifth volume of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, published in 1927, takes up erotic symbolism, the mechanism of detumescence, and the psychic state in pregnancy. Ellis groups under symbolism a wide range of sexual variations, arguing that they share a common root in the way desire fastens on images, objects, and acts.

Case notes, medical reports, and historical examples fill the pages, from fetishism to the dreams and delusions of patients in asylums. The closing study turns to pregnancy, tracing changes of mood and mind in expectant mothers. Ellis writes with the same cool, systematic manner as in earlier volumes, aiming to replace moral judgment with description and explanation.
13750-the-heavenly-footman-or-a-descript:
John Bunyan wrote The Heavenly Footman as a short guide to earnest Christian life. The title pictures the believer as a runner in a race, urged to run so as to obtain the prize. Bunyan opens with an epistle to slothful and careless people. He warns that desire alone kills the slothful, and that wasted time shames the soul.

Chapters compare earthly racing with the race for heaven. Runners must press on, not merely start well. Bunyan uses plain images from sport, harvest, and daily work. The style is direct and urgent, in the manner of Pilgrim's Progress. The tract suits readers of Puritan devotion and Bunyan's plain theology.
13941-the-divine-right-of-church-governm:
Sundry ministers of Christ within London wrote this treatise on the divine right of Presbyterian church government. A new, corrected edition argues that preaching and ruling elders, in sessional, presbyterial, and synodical assemblies, hold the only lawful divine claim. Scripture, the authors hold, warrants that order alone. An appendix adds extracts on church membership and ministry.

The appendix treats scriptural qualifications of members, ministers' sole right to preach, and the people's right to choose pastors. Earlier writers had vindicated parts of church government, but none, the authors claim, had laid open divine right as a system. The book belongs to seventeenth-century Presbyterian polemic. It suits students of church polity and Puritan thought.
13958-the-authoritative-life-of-general-:
G. S. Railton, first commissioner to General Booth, wrote this authoritative life of the Salvation Army's founder. William Booth, born April 10, 1829, died August 20, 1912. Chapters follow childhood poverty, salvation in youth, lay ministry, and early ministry. Fight against formality, revivalism, and the East London beginning follow.

Later chapters cover army-making, army leading, desperate fighting, and growth in America and Australasia. Railton, with a preface by Bramwell Booth, writes as an insider. He shows Booth building a disciplined, uniformed Christian mission. The book suits readers of religious and social history. It remains the standard early life of Booth.
14590-a-new-hochelagan-burying-ground-di:
W. D. Lighthall's 1898 privately printed notes report a newly found Hochelagan burying ground at Westmount, on the western spur of Mount Royal in Montreal, discovered between July and September 1898. The title calls itself provisional on the term Hochelagan.

The ground, probably of the people of old Hochelaga or their Mohawk kin, held powerful men in their prime and one young woman. Large stones lay above the bodies, and flat stones had served as scoops. The plateau, sheltered and sunny, suited corn and beans. The notes are a careful early record of Montreal archaeology.
14902-deadwood-dick-the-prince-of-the-ro:
Edward L. Wheeler's 1877 dime novel, number one in Beadle's Half Dime Library, introduces Deadwood Dick, prince of the road and black rider of the Black Hills. Fearless Frank comes to the rescue as the story opens on the plains midway between Cheyenne and the Black Hills.

A wagon train has halted for a noonday feed, not a railway train but white-covered prairie schooners drawn by strong mules, drawn in a circle about a campfire roasting venison. Rough, bearded men gather round, with one exception. Wheeler writes western adventure at full gallop: outlaws, rescues and a masked rider who would run through many sequels.
15126-lecture-on-the-aborigines-of-newfo:
Joseph Noad, surveyor-general of Newfoundland, gave this lecture at St. John's Mechanics' Institute in January 1859, and it was printed there the same year. He opens with rival theories of where North America's native peoples came from, weighing Tatar, lost-tribe, and northeast Asian origins. The Asian route, he notes, was the view most often held.

Noad then turns to Newfoundland's own native people, the Beothuk, and to what was known of their life and fate. His tone is that of a colonial official speaking to a learned local crowd. Read today, the lecture is both a source on Beothuk history and a record of Victorian ideas about race and origins.
15171-journals-of-travels-in-assam-burma:
William Griffith's journals, arranged by John McClelland from an 1847 edition, record travels in Assam, Burma, Bhutan, Afghanistan, and nearby lands. Chapters follow an Assam deputation to examine the tea plant, a Mishmee mountain excursion, and journeys from Upper Assam toward Ava and Rangoon. Plant notes fill many pages.

Griffith, a botanist, writes with a naturalist's eye for tea sites, river routes, and plant distribution, alongside travel hardship. A Linnaean Society notice fronts the book. Scholars of botany, empire, and Asian travel will find the journals detailed, rugged, and rich in firsthand observation.
15188-the-outdoor-chums-after-big-game-o:
Captain Quincy Allen's 1911 Outdoor Chums book sends the Rod, Gun and Camera Club after big game in the wilderness. A frontispiece shows a beast galloping in mad rage straight toward the boys. Chapters open with glorious news, motorcycle thieves, and a moonlit ride home, then start Hank right and head west.

Perilous adventures follow: hunts, camps, and narrow escapes, told in the brisk series style for boys. The chums use pluck, friendship, and outdoor skill to pull through. Young readers who like hunting tales and camp stories will enjoy the book's pace, even where its views of game now feel dated.
15401-the-great-lone-land-a-narrative-of:
Colonel W. F. Butler published this narrative of travel in the North-West of America in 1872, with a route map. The preface opens at York Factory on Hudson Bay, with a man resolved to write a book of all he had seen, and all he had not seen. Butler then tells his own journey west, in a land of rivers, plains, and distant settlements.

Chapters cross the Atlantic, pass through Boston, New York, Niagara, and Quebec, and push on to the Red River country. There Butler meets the half-breeds, the early settlers, and Louis Riel, and recounts the Red River revolt and the murder of Scott. The book blends adventure, report, and reflection on a frontier changing hands. It remains a vivid firsthand account of the Canadian West just as it opened to new rule.
15599-the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bie:
This eighth volume of the collected works of Ambrose Bierce first appeared in 1911. Gordian Press reprinted it in New York in 1966. It gathers negligible tales, On with the Dance, and epigrams. The contents divide into tale groups: negligible tales, the parenticide club, the fourth estate, and the ocean wave, followed by a review section.

Negligible tales include a bottomless grave, Jupiter Doke brigadier-general, the widower Turmore, and the city of the gone away. The parenticide club offers my favorite murder, oil of dog, and the hypnotist. The fourth estate satirizes journalists and the press, while the ocean wave gives shipwreck tales and a captain of the Camel. On with the Dance reviews letters and life with Bierce's bite. The volume shows his dark wit at full stretch: irony, horror, and satire in short, sharp form.
15694-a-friend-of-c-sar-a-tale-of-the-fa:
William Stearns Davis published this tale of the fall of the Roman Republic, set in 50 to 47 B.C., in New York in 1900, with Grosset and Dunlap. An epigraph from Vergil reminds Romans that theirs is the art of ruling peoples, sparing the weak, and flinging the haughty from high seats. Davis dedicates the book to his father, William Vail Wilson Davis, who taught him more than all his books.

Contents run from Praeneste and the upper walks of society through the privilege of a vestal, Pompeius Magnus, and Agias's adventure to the great proconsul and the new consuls. The seventh of January, the Rubicon, and the profitable career of Gabinius follow. Cleopatra enters late. Davis writes a historical novel of Caesar's rise and the Republic's fall, seen through a friend's eyes, with politics, war, and love in the last years of Rome.
1576-a-unique-story-of-a-marvellous-care:
Joel Benton tells the life of Phineas T. Barnum, the showman who built the American museum, the circus, and a career of marvels. Barnum's freak shows, hoaxes, and promotions made him famous on two continents. Barnum, born in 1810, built his American Museum in New York in the 1840s.

Benton follows Barnum from Connecticut shopkeeping to great wealth, politics, and philanthropy, stressing his energy and humour. The life gives a lively portrait of a man who turned wonder into business. His circus, later joined with Bailey's, became the Greatest Show on Earth.
15911-narrative-of-a-voyage-to-the-north:
A personal narrative by Gabriel Franchere of a voyage to the Northwest Coast in 1811 to 1814, or the first American settlement on the Pacific. J. V. Huntington translated and edited the work, issued by Redfield in New York in 1854. An illustration shows Astoria as it was in 1813. Franchere writes as a witness, with spelling and style kept as in his own hand.

Franchere sailed with the Astor expedition to found a fur post at the Columbia's mouth. Hardships, native peoples, and rival traders fill his account. Astoria's rise and fall unfold through daily detail. The narrative stands as a firsthand record of America's Pacific beginning: brave, rough, and far from home.
15966-a-voyage-of-consolation-being-in-t:
A travel novel by Sara Jeannette Duncan, writing as Mrs. Everard Cotes, in a uniform edition with her other books. A Voyage of Consolation follows A Social Departure, in which Orthodocia and her friend went round the world by themselves. Duncan, a Canadian wit, writes of travel with humour and sharp eyes. The book was issued in cloth at one dollar and fifty cents.

The voyage offers consolation after sorrow, with new lands, new friends, and old jokes renewed. Duncan's heroines talk, observe, and laugh their way across seas. The tone stays bright and companionable. The novel delights as a sequel for readers who loved the first voyage: the same brave girls, a wider world, and comfort found in going on.
16017-the-poor-scholar-traits-and-storie:
William Carleton's tale opens in bitter November weather on a barren Irish hill called Esker Dhu. Dominick M'Evoy and his son Jemmy dig potatoes in thin clothes while sleet drives across the slope. The old man, worn by years of rack-rent farming on poor soil, can barely keep at his toil. The son bears the cold better, but both must turn their sides to each storm gust.

From that hard farm life grows the story of a poor scholar, a young man whose learning sets him apart from the labor around him. Carleton writes with sympathy for Irish cottagers and anger at the rents that grind them down. The tale offers a vivid, human picture of poverty, schooling, and family duty in rural Ireland.
16276-the-power-of-faith-exemplified-in-:
This new edition of The Power of Faith tells the life and writings of Mrs. Isabella Graham, enriched by her narrative of her husband's death and other letters. Entered in 1843 by Joanna Bethune and published by the American Tract Society in New York and Boston, the book opens with Graham's early life and residence in Canada. Birth, schooling, conversion, marriage, and a voyage to Quebec lay the foundation of her character.

Later chapters follow her widowhood, charity, and faith in action, with Proverbs on humility and the widow's border as its text. Graham became a model of evangelical benevolence in early America. Readers of religious biography will find an earnest, moving portrait of piety put to work.
17075-dialogue-of-comfort-against-tribul:
St. Thomas More's Dialogue of Comfort Against Tribulation is a long talk on how to bear trouble with faith and calm. This 1951 Sheed and Ward edition keeps the 1557 text whole while easing its old spelling, word order, and stale words for modern readers. Monica Stevens made the changes, and nothing was cut or added beyond small linking words.

The talk moves through fear, pain, loss, and death, testing each worry against reason and trust in God. Its slow, patient back-and-forth suits readers who want counsel rather than quick comfort. Even in plain modern dress, the work keeps its old voice: grave, kind, and firm about facing hard days without despair.
17592-a-narrative-of-the-expedition-to-d:
An American in the service of the Viceroy of Egypt wrote this narrative of the expedition to Dongola and Sennaar. It went under the command of Ismael Pasha, undertaken by order of Mehemmed Ali Pasha, Viceroy of Egypt. The book was published in London in 1822 by John Murray of Albemarle Street. Its author dedicates the work to Henry Salt, the British consul general in Egypt, calling him a fatherly friend in a foreign land.

The narrative was also recommended to the care of John William Bankes. Readers get an early eyewitness account of Egypt's southward expansion into Nubia and Sudan, by a participant. The book suits readers of African exploration and of Mehemmed Ali's Egypt.
17971-the-abolition-of-slavery-the-right:
William Lloyd Garrison and others put together this pamphlet on the abolition of slavery and the government's right under the war power. It opens with extracts from John Quincy Adams's speech of April 1842 on war with Britain and Mexico, and it argues from his words.

Adams held that Congress could not meddle with slavery in peace, but that war changed the case, since the nation's peace and welfare were at stake. The pamphlet presses that logic toward emancipation by war power. It is a short, sharp abolitionist tract, and a key text for readers who trace how the war power argument freed the slaves.
18392-thoughts-i-met-on-the-highway-word:
Ralph Waldo Trine, author of In Tune with the Infinite, published this book of friendly cheer in 1919 with Dodd, Mead in New York, copyrighted in 1912. Thoughts I Met on the Highway gathers selections from Trine's Life Books, one volume of selections for each week of the year. Trine's message runs through all his books: thoughts are forces, like builds like, and like attracts like.

The volume offers short pieces for the road: the winning of the best, the greatest thing ever known, every living creature, character building, and thought power. Trine writes for readers who want a daily lift, not a system: brief, warm counsels on living with courage, kindness, and hope. Readers get a pocket companion of New Thought: plain sentences meant to be read slowly, one a day, and carried onto the highway of ordinary life.
18531-timothy-s-quest-a-story-for-anybod:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this story for anybody, young or old, who cares to read it. Wiggin also wrote The Birds' Christmas Carol and The Story of Patsy. Houghton, Mifflin published it in Boston and New York, with copyright in 1890. Timothy's Quest is told in scenes, like a play for the home, and the thirty-seventh thousand printing shows its long popularity.

Scene one gives Flossy Morrison learning the secret of death without ever having learned the secret of life. Scene two gives little Timothy Jessup assuming parental responsibilities. Later scenes show Timothy planning a campaign with providence assisting. Jabe Slocum acts as guardian angel. Timothy finds a house where he thinks a baby is needed, though the inmates do not entirely agree. Readers get a Wiggin tale of orphans, kindness, and a child's quest for a home.
18975-the-north-pole-its-discovery-in-19:
Robert E. Peary wrote this 1910 account of reaching the North Pole in 1909 under the Peary Arctic Club. Theodore Roosevelt wrote an introduction and Gilbert H. Grosvenor a foreword, and the book carries flags borne on the final dash. Peary sets his own trek inside a long history of polar tries.

He reviews Parry and other early explorers, then tells of ice, sledges, dogs, and the hard push north from a land base. Cold, drift, and open water test men and plans at each stage. Readers get the explorer's own case for his claim, plus a survey of how Arctic travel changed over time.
19156-the-continental-monthly-vol-iii-is:
This June 1863 issue of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy, continues a defence of the Union in its second part. It contrasts the Union's upward path with the pro-slavery rebellion and its tendencies, tracing mankind's slow rise through revolution and faith toward a higher, more united life.

The writer argues that advancing civilisation multiplies and organises human bonds, while immoral, ignorant, indolent communities lapse toward disintegration and petty states. Such evil, he claims, corrects itself. Readers get a wartime Northern magazine essay, earnest, philosophical, and firm for Union.
19221-the-golden-treasury-of-the-best-so:
Francis Turner Palgrave selected this Golden Treasury of the best songs and lyrical poems in the English language, with pictures by A. Pearse. Dedicated to Alfred Tennyson, it recalls Henry Hallam, whose just judgment and patriotism Palgrave praises, and notes Tennyson's encouragement on walks at Treryn Dinas. The book aims to be a true national anthology.

Poems range from Drummond of Hawthornden on spring and love to Shakespeare on time and love, with lyrics chosen for beauty and lasting power. Readers get a classic anthology of English lyric verse across three centuries, still a fine introduction to the tradition.
19314-raphael-a-collection-of-fifteen-pi:
Estelle M. Hurll edited this 1899 art book on Raphael, with fifteen pictures and a portrait painted by himself. It opens with his character as an artist, books of reference, a directory of pictures, collateral reading, and a table of his life and contemporaries. Each picture then gets an introduction and reading.

Abraham and the Three Angels shows Abraham bowing low in Oriental robes, offering water, bread, and a calf under a tree, while Sarah peeps through a door at the mysterious guests. Hurll reads courtesy as honour craved, not favour given. Readers get a gentle guide to Raphael for home study.
19332-michael-angelo-buonarroti-with-tra:
Charles Holroyd, keeper of the National Gallery of British Art, wrote this 1903 life of Michelangelo, with translations of Condivi's life and three dialogues from the Portuguese by Francisco d'Ollanda. Plates show the David, the Pieta, the Battle of the Centaurs, and the Day of Judgment. The book is a scholarly tribute.

Young Michelangelo copies a faun so well that Lorenzo the Magnificent jokes that an old faun should lack teeth, so the boy cuts one tooth away and drills its root hole. Lorenzo then takes him into favour. Readers get a rich, illustrated life of a Renaissance master, artist, and man.
19470-yorkshire-lyrics-poems-written-in-:
John Hartley wrote this set of Yorkshire lyrics, in the dialect spoken in the West Riding, with a selection of fugitive verses in plain English added. Hartley, known for his Clock Almanack and Yorkshire Tales, writes of home life, work, and local characters in the voice of his county.

The dialect poems carry the book's heart: humor, pathos, and pride in Yorkshire speech. For readers outside the Riding, the verses offer both a glossary-free plunge into northern talk and a record of a spoken culture that print rarely caught.
19731-under-the-ocean-to-the-south-pole-:
Roy Rockwood was a house name for boys' adventure series books. Under the Ocean to the South Pole, from 1907, sends the submarine Wonder on a strange cruise. A scientist in the opening scene tightens bolts on a wild apparatus. He hopes aloud that the vessel will work as planned. His young friend Mark shares the doubt and the thrill.

Submarine polar voyages were fresh fantasy in 1907. No real submarine had yet cruised under polar ice. Rockwood's books mixed invention talk with constant peril. Storms, ice, and strange seas tested the young crew. Series readers returned for each new impossible trip. The Wonder books show early science fiction aimed squarely at boys.
1988-the-history-of-tom-thumb-to-which-a:
This old English chapbook tells the story of Tom Thumb, the tiny boy given to a childless ploughman and his wife by the magician Merlin. Set in the days of King Arthur, it follows a hero no bigger than a thumb through a world built for full-sized folk. Tom Thumb tales circulated for centuries in cheap print, passed from teller to teller before they reached books.

Tom survives scrapes with animals, courts, and kitchens, and two short tales follow: one of a cat and a mouse, and one of a cry of fire. The style is simple and direct, made for reading aloud to children. Children enjoy the scale jokes most, as Tom hides in puddings, rides mice, and outwits creatures far larger than himself.
20110-canada-the-empire-of-the-north-bei:
Agnes C. Laut published Canada: The Empire of the North in 1909. Her subtitle calls it the romantic story of Canada's growth. The book traces Canada from colony to kingdom, in her bold phrase. For twenty years, she notes, Canada's population barely grew at all.

Laut promises the tale itself will explain that long stall. She then asks what fast growth, like that in the United States, might bring. Tables of numbers sit beside tales of trade, fur, and settlement. Readers get a proud, sweeping history written when Canada's boom had just begun.
20617-young-wild-west-at-forbidden-pass-:

23340-campaigns-of-a-non-combatant-and-h:

23450-the-book-of-ornamental-alphabets-a:

5204-the-inns-and-taverns-of-pickwick-wi:

doe-osti-3453387-modelling-external-tran: Transonic flight — right around the speed of sound — is where shock waves start to bite. from-london-to-land-s-end-and-two-letter:
Daniel Defoe's From London to Land's End, printed by Cassell in 1888, collects letters from his Tour through the whole island of Great Britain. The introduction warns that two letters from another gentleman's similar Journey are appended, and that mixed sets often confuse purchasers. Defoe's own letters march west through southern England.

He describes towns, trade, ruins, and curiosities with a journalist's appetite: Portland nearly an island, its beach joining the shore, and Abbotsbury famous now only for its abbey ruins. Defoe traveled as a government agent and merchant as much as an author. His Tour remains a prime source for England's economy and landscape in the 1720s, brisk and opinionated on every page.
govdocs-archive_org-MasonicTempleToPadre:
A special edition of the Italian Catholic journal Chiesa viva, number 381 of March 2006, asks whether the new church of St. Padre Pio is in fact a Masonic temple. Franco Adessa, with Father Luigi Villa, presents the case. The church at San Giovanni Rotondo, Padre Pio's town, had opened in 2004 to designs by Renzo Piano.

The authors read the building's forms, numbers, and symbols as Masonic signs hidden in a Catholic shrine. Theirs is a traditionalist polemic, richly illustrated and wholly convinced. The edition is held as it appeared: an artifact of the quarrels over modern church design and the memory of Italy's most loved modern saint.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIADowneyJohnT_:
John T. Downey was a CIA officer whose plane was shot down over China in 1952, on a mission connected with an agent extraction. Captured and sentenced to life, he spent twenty years in Chinese prisons. This Washington Post article by Thomas O'Toole, dated March 18, 1973, meets him coming home.

Downey's release came with the Nixon opening to China, and he walked out the longest-held prisoner of the CIA's early Cold War. O'Toole tells the capture, the decades in which Washington denied he was an intelligence officer, and the return. The article is the homecoming chapter of a famous spy case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarksSidTheWatl:
Sid Marks told the FBI a short story from November 23, 1963, the day after the assassination. He was in the offices of detective Dick Hathcock when Hathcock's associate, Roy Payne, came in. Payne asked whether anyone had been in to get a rifle. The bureau wrote the account up as a report, filed as LA 89-75 and known here as the Watley Report.

Reports like this one fill the assassination files by the thousand. Each preserves a single odd remark or errand that might matter. A question about a rifle, asked the day after the shooting, was exactly the kind of detail agents were told to record. The report keeps the wording, the office, and the date.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NelsonJohnT_Nel:
Harold Weisberg wrote to John T. Nelson of New Orleans on November 23, 1970. A Times-Picayune story had quoted Weisberg, and the letter takes that story as its starting point. Weisberg also describes his own independent investigations of political assassinations in New Orleans.

New Orleans was the second front of assassination research, home to the Garrison inquiry and to many Oswald leads. Weisberg worked the city by correspondence, correcting newspapers and trading findings with local contacts. The letter to Nelson shows that work at desk level: a clipping received, a reply drafted, a claim about his investigations restated for the record. It also dates his New Orleans inquiries to at least 1970.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NoguchiThomasT_: Thomas TNoguchi - the coroner to the stars - lends his name to this declassified US government file at the Internet Archive. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TranscriptsWash: On May 19, 1974, the Washington Post printed another White House tape transcript, the sixth in its series. govdocs-archive_org-the-esoteric-hitleri: The Esoteric Hitlerism of Jason Alfred Thompkins 3rd: the volume - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-theoretical-biophysi: Dakota Frandsen published a 2026 study of an alleged 1993 incident involving Soviet soldiers. Its long title uses dense terms from physics and earth science. govdocs-archive_org-understanding-realit:
Chang Po-tuan, a Song-dynasty master, wrote Understanding Reality in the eleventh century as a classic of Taoist internal alchemy. The text is presented here with commentary.

Internal alchemy treats the body itself as the furnace: breath, essence, and spirit are refined into an inner elixir, the Tao made real in a person. Chang's verses are dense and coded, which is why commentary travels with them. The work is a cornerstone of Taoist literature. Readers of Chinese religion meet in it one of the tradition's most studied guides to the inner path.
history-of-the-conquest-of-peru-with-a-p:
William Hickling Prescott's Conquest of Peru appears in this fuller version with its footnotes and a preliminary view of the civilization of the Incas, as its companion headnote explains. The preface again describes the nearly blind historian's apparatus: notes in hieroglyphic characters, a blind man's writing-case, and a secretary grown expert at reading both. The same Claudian and Lope de Vega mottoes open the work.

The preliminary view surveys Inca government, religion, agriculture, and arts before Pizarro lands. Churches built of ancient stones, altars raised where the sun's image shone, show the conquest's layering in the middle books. With notes intact, this edition serves readers who want Prescott's evidence as well as his narrative.
home-vegetable-gardening-a-complete-and-:
F. F. Rockwell's Home Vegetable Gardening is a complete and practical guide to planting and caring for vegetables, fruits and berries worth growing at home. Rockwell writes as first aid for gardeners whose experience is narrow and whose spare time is limited.

High prices make the home garden a great help, Rockwell notes, as well as a hobby, and his aim is practical, efficient gardening with the least fuss and loss of time. Garden books, he observes, seldom lack information but often fail to present it clearly. His volume tries to be comprehensive yet simple and concise. Home gardeners will find it a sensible, old-fashioned manual that still earns its place.
journals-of-travels-in-assam-burma-bhoot:
William Griffith's Journals of Travels record journeys in Assam, Burma, Bhootan, Afghanistan, and nearby countries. John M'Clelland arranged the journals for publication, in an edition from 1847. The contents open with a notice of Griffith's life from the Linnaean Society. His first journey went with the Assam deputation examining the tea plant.

Later chapters cross the Mishmee mountains and the tea districts of Upper Assam. Griffith traveled toward Hookum and on to Ava, noting plants as he went. He descended the Irrawaddi to Rangoon and journeyed into Bootan with notes on plant distribution. As a botanist, Griffith filled his travel diary with the plants of each region. The journals mix mission travel, science, and close natural observation.
lecture-on-the-aborigines-of-newfoundlan:
Joseph Noad delivered this lecture on the aborigines of Newfoundland in January 1859. He spoke before the Mechanics' Institute at St. John's. Noad served as surveyor-general of the colony.

R. J. Parsons printed the lecture at St. John's that year. Noad surveys rival theories about the island's first people. His office gave him wide knowledge of Newfoundland's coasts and interior. The Beothuk and other peoples stand behind his inquiry. The lecture preserves early colonial thinking about Indigenous history, with its limits. Mechanics' institutes brought lectures to working audiences then. Noad's talk joined local pride to early anthropology.
legends-of-the-middle-ages-narrated-with:
H. A. Guerber narrated Legends of the Middle Ages in 1896. Her subtitle stresses links with literature and art. She dedicated the book to her sister Adele.

Old lines about Arthur and Charlemagne open her preface. Roland's fights with Saracens stand among her chosen tales. Guerber built the book for students meeting medieval romance. Clear retelling matters more to her than scholarly dispute. Teachers used her legends to lead young readers toward the great originals. Siegfried, Beowulf, and the Nibelungs enter her survey too. Art works named in the text guide museum visits.
life-letters-and-epicurean-philosophy-of:
Ninon de l'Enclos, famed beauty of seventeenth-century France, fills this 1903 volume. Robinson and Overton published the life, letters, and philosophy together. Early chapters weigh Ninon as a standard and as a parallel. Her youth and the morals of her period follow.

Count de Coligny enters the story of her early attachments. The Birds of the Tournelles nickname her circle of admirers. Her mother's death marks a turning point in the narrative. The letters let readers judge her celebrated wit for themselves. Her mother's death changes the household's course in the biography. Later chapters follow Ninon's salon fame and her written philosophy.
michael-angelo-buonarroti-with-translati:
Charles Holroyd, keeper of the National Gallery of British Art, published this study of Michelangelo in 1903. Alongside his own account, Holroyd prints translations of two early sources. The first is the life of the master written by his pupil Ascanio Condivi. The second is three dialogues from the Portuguese of Francisco d'Ollanda.

Plates reproduce the David, the Moses, the Pietà, and scenes from the Sistine ceiling. Readers can thus compare the Renaissance testimony with the works themselves. Condivi knew Michelangelo personally, so his biography carries unusual weight. The volume serves students who want both the art and the earliest written record of its maker.
morien-a-metrical-romance-rendered-into-:
Jessie L. Weston rendered this Arthurian romance into English prose from the medieval Dutch. It is number four in her Arthurian Romances series. Her preface explains the source: a metrical romance inside the Dutch version of the Lancelot. There it runs past five thousand lines, closing the compilation's first volume.

So far as anyone knows, the romance survives nowhere else. Neither its date nor its author is known; the manuscript is early fourteenth century. Morien is a Moorish knight who comes to Arthur's court seeking his father. Weston, a leading Arthurian scholar, compared such compilations to Malory's, and her translation rescued a unique tale.
mountain-pictures-and-other-poems-part-2:
John Greenleaf Whittier's poems of nature fill this part of his collected works. The Mountain Pictures sequence opens the selection. Its two parts view Franconia from the Pemigewasset and Monadnock from Wachuset. Whittier hails the mountains of the North, asking them to unveil their brows once more.

Other poems include The Vanishers, The Pressed Gentian, and Sunset on the Bearcamp. The Trailing Arbutus, Storm on Lake Asquam, and A Summer Pilgrimage follow. Whittier, the Quaker poet of New England, mixes exact local scenery with religious feeling. These nature poems sit beside subjective and religious pieces in the same gathered volume.
narrative-of-a-voyage-to-the-northwest-c:
Gabriel Franchere tells of the first American settlement on the Pacific. His voyage covered 1811 through 1814 on the Northwest Coast. J. V. Huntington translated and edited the book. Redfield issued it in New York in 1854.

A picture shows Astoria as it stood in 1813. Senator Thomas Benton quoted the book in an 1846 Senate speech. He called it the fullest, most trusted source on Oregon's claims. Franchere, a British subject on the Columbia, wrote without slant, Benton said. The tale covers the Tonquin, the post's founding, and its fall in war, by an eyewitness clerk.
nasa-tm-19650020356-auroral-particles-fr:
T W Speiser at Goddard wrote this first paper on where auroral particles come from. The aurora is lit by charged particles striking the upper air. Many are thought to arrive from the geomagnetic tail, the long part of Earth's magnetic field blown away from the Sun. Speiser follows particle paths near a neutral sheet in that tail.

Field models are used to predict how the particles behave. Their paths decide where they enter the air and light the sky. The paper is marked part one, so a series was planned. It reflects early work on a question that satellite data were only beginning to answer.
nasa-tm-19660021056-fin-a-computer-progr:
FIN is the name of a computer program described in this April 1966 Goddard report, numbered X-721-66-162. The program calculates the aerodynamic characteristics of fins at supersonic speeds. Fins guide rockets and missiles, and their lift and drag must be known before flight. A program can sweep through many fin shapes and speeds far faster than tunnel testing can.

Each tunnel run costs time and money, and models must be built by hand. A checked program lets designers discard weak shapes early. The best few can then go to the tunnel for proof. Program reports like this one spread a single tool to every design office that needed fin data in the Saturn and missile era.
nasa-tm-19670009440-simultaneous-cloud-a:
B. A. Sparkman and G. T. Cherrix, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this preliminary report in February 1967. It presents cloud albedo measurements, measures of how much sunlight a surface reflects, taken at the same time from aircraft and from orbit. Matching the readings of different instruments was the point of the exercise.

Aircraft carried Sol-A-Meters and a medium resolution infrared radiometer, while the Nimbus II satellite measured with its own radiometer from space. The teams measured the reflectivity of clouds, desert, and ocean surfaces simultaneously. Instrument descriptions, the measurement method, and the data fill the short report. Good agreement was found among the coordinated measurements from all of the instruments, the abstract reports, which supported using the satellite readings with confidence.
nasa-tm-19670016998-stress-and-stability:
K. Schiffner wrote this study in German, published in April 1966 as a German aerospace research report. It investigates stress and stability in thin-wall conical shells under loads that are the same all around the axis. Cone-shaped shells appear often in rocket structures, where buckling under load can destroy a vehicle. The English translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, in January 1967.

Schiffner applies a nonlinear shell theory that allows large deformations. The first part describes the shell's unbuckled state under axial load and internal pressure, solving the governing equations by a refined difference method. An exact solution is also given for the simplified linear case. The second part computes buckling loads as an eigenvalue problem, solved step by step. Effects of shell proportions and of slight pre-deformation are discussed. Results agreed well with experiments, especially for axial load with high internal pressure.
nasa-tm-19670018236-galactic-x-rays-a-su:
Elihu Boldt, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this summary in May 1967. It was prepared for the 1968 Yearbook of Science and Technology, published by McGraw-Hill. The subject is galactic X-rays, high-energy radiation arriving from sources inside our own galaxy, a field then only five years old.

Rocket observations of solar X-rays had run for about twenty years, Boldt notes, but galactic X-ray astronomy began in 1962. A rocket team hunting lunar X-rays instead detected a strong source in Scorpius, named Sco X-1, outshining the quiet Sun at short wavelengths. Since then, rocket and balloon experiments had found at least thirty more discrete galactic sources. Balloons lift instruments above most of the atmosphere, and rockets go higher still. The summary reports the field's status just before the OSO-III satellite carried the first successful X-ray telescope into orbit in March 1967.
nasa-tm-19680018177-a-noncontacting-disp:
Eugene C. Naumann and Bruce Flagge of Langley Research Center present a displacement measuring technique that never touches the test object in this October 1966 conference paper. Vibration testing needs exact records of how parts move. Contact sensors can disturb light structures or fail under harsh shaking.

Flagge's part of the paper covers the instrumentation technique itself. Naumann's part covers its application to current vibration testing at Langley. The method measures displacement without contact, so the sensor adds no load to the structure. Engineers could thus record true motion during vibration tests. The paper was given at the Instrument Society of America conference in New York.
nasa-tm-19680026117-proton-and-ultra-vio:
C. A. Nicoletta of Goddard Space Flight Center reports irradiation tests on the RAE-A satellite's target sphere material in this August 1968 report. The material is zinc titanate over Lexan. Space radiation can darken such coatings and change how much sunlight they absorb.

One-inch samples were exposed to low energy protons, then to protons and ultraviolet light in sequence. A purpose-built system allowed optical reflectance measurements without removing the samples. Very little degradation appeared below a threshold proton flux. Above that threshold, solar absorptance rose rapidly, more so for the higher energy beam. Combined proton and ultraviolet exposure enhanced damage at first, then leveled off at higher fluxes.
nasa-tm-19700005739-stress-corrosion-cra:
James G. Williamson of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on November 19, 1969. Its subject is stress corrosion cracking in one titanium alloy, Ti-6Al-4V. That kind of cracking can grow in a stressed metal when it touches certain fluids.

Williamson reports tests of the alloy in a range of fluids. The point was to learn which fluids attack the metal and how the damage grows. Builders of rockets and aircraft used such test results to judge where the alloy could serve safely and which fluids it had to avoid.
nasa-tm-19700020684-the-compressible-flo:
Robert E. Henry of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 heat transfer meeting in Monterey, California. It studies mixtures of two components in two phases as they rush through nozzles and orifices. Such mixtures mix gas and liquid in a single fast stream.

Henry builds a math model of the fastest discharge such a stream can reach. The model accounts for heat and push passing between the gas and liquid parts. It predicts the key pressure ratio and the flow rate from the starting conditions. Its results matched published air and water nozzle data well. He then extends the same model to flow through orifices.
nasa-tm-19700026456-convergence-accelera:
Speeding the convergence of the steepest descent method is the aim of this Houston internal note, number MSC-ED-R-67-52. It was issued by the Manned Spacecraft Center there. That method is a step-by-step way to find the best value of a problem, used here for flight path optimization work.

The note first defines the optimization problem and reviews earlier gradient methods as background. It then builds the gradient method twice, once under hard constraints and once under soft ones. For each form, a matching acceleration procedure follows, meant to reach the answer in fewer steps. An application with results tests the procedures, and appendices supply orbit parameters, the governing equations, and a worked example.
nasa-tm-19720002555-a-compilation-of-res:
A NASA preprint numbered X-752-71-351 compiles results on the behavior of phase locked loops; its author names are garbled in the scan. Phase locked loops are circuits that lock an oscillator onto an incoming signal. They sit inside radios, tracking receivers, and spacecraft communications gear.

The volume sums up the state of the art for engineers who design with these loops. A terminology section fixes working definitions, and an index organizes the compiled results. Results are grouped by their describing equations and by the jobs loops do: acquisition, tracking, and detection. Each result is presented with its assumptions and source references. An example problem works the methods end to end, and a closing section points to future work.
nasa-tm-19720004463-graphic-displays-for:
Daniel L Whipple of the Lewis Research Center described a display system for large test facilities in November 1971, as NASA TM X-67968. Wind tunnel crews once waited for printed results after each run. Whipple's system put live data on screens in the control room. It joined new software with display hardware on a shared computer. Engineers could watch a test unfold and react at once.

Users could call up numbers or graphs as they wished. Hard copy printouts were available from the same screens. Helper programs allowed editing of graphics while the test ran. They also handled program control, data changes, and later microfilm output. The setup brought interactive computing into daily tunnel work.
nasa-tm-19720019561-application-of-an-on:
W. N. Stewart and colleagues wrote this NASA preprint, numbered X-715-72-226, on putting a real computer aboard the OAO C spacecraft. OAO was the Orbiting Astronomical Observatory series, and OAO C was its fourth spacecraft. The machine they describe, called OBP 1, is a stored-program computer built for spacecraft use.

The abstract describes a medium-scale machine that works in parallel and holds more than sixteen thousand words of memory, running on modest power. Aboard OAO C its jobs would include storing commands, monitoring the spacecraft, and reporting malfunctions. It would also compress data, summarize status, and possibly take emergency corrective action in some abnormal situations. The report covers the computer's history, its interfaces with the spacecraft, and its memory, processor, and input-output units in detail.
nomads-of-the-north-a-story-of-romance-a:
James Oliver Curwood called Nomads of the North a story of romance and adventure under the open stars. It opens in late March, at the dying out of the Eagle Moon. Neewa, a black bear cub, gets his first real look at the world that month.

His mother Noozak is an old bear, full of rheumatics and a wish to sleep late. She slept four months that winter, not the usual three, in a cavern on a high, barren ridge. Neewa was born while she slept soundly. From the den he looks down on a valley between Jackson's Knee and the Shamattawa River, as early spring works its change.
occasional-papers-selected-from-the-guar:
Richard William Church wrote essays for three major papers. They appeared in the Guardian, the Times, and the Saturday Review. The pieces date from 1846 to 1890. Volume two was printed in London in 1897. Church had served as Dean of Saint Paul's.

The contents focus on church and state in Victorian England. Essays treat Gladstone, court judgments, and disendowment of the church. Other pieces review books by Renan and other writers. Church writes as a careful churchman and critic. The volume preserves informed debate from a long career. Later pieces treat new courts and church reform plans in detail.
outlines-of-lessons-in-botany-part-i-fro: Jane H. Newell's Outlines of Lessons in Botany is a teaching manual from 1888. Part One runs From Seed to Leaf. Teachers, or mothers studying with their children, are its audience. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. The course opens with plants and their uses. Seedlings raised in the schoolroom follow, then roots and root-hairs. Buds and branches close the part. No lesson text appears.
over-the-top-by-an-american-soldier-who-:
Arthur Guy Empey was an American who enlisted in the British army. He served as a machine gunner in France. Over the Top came out of the trenches. By its twenty-sixth impression it was America's most famous soldier's book of the war. It comes together with Tommy's Dictionary of the Trenches, his glossary of the soldiers' slang.

His foreword argues the Allied cause from sixteen years of roughing it around the world, before the mast and in the trenches. The average American, he says, mistakes the Englishman for a distant, humorless man; Tommy Atkins proved himself the best of mates, bubbling with humor, willing to sacrifice everything but honor. Empey's book sold the British Tommy to America in Tommy's own voice.
raphael-a-collection-of-fifteen-pictures: Raphael, a collection of fifteen pictures and a portrait of the painter, edited by Estelle M. Hurll in the Masterpieces of Art series, was published at Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin Company with an 1899 copyright. The pages shown give the contents. Raphael's self-portrait serves as frontispiece. It comes from a photograph by Fratelli Alinari. Sections on his character as an artist follow. Books of reference come next. A historical directory of the pictures appears. Collateral reading, an outline of his life, and his contemporaries close the list.
sanders-union-fourth-reader-embracing-a-:
Charles W. Sanders, A.M., wrote Sanders' Union Fourth Reader, embracing a full exposition of the principles of rhetorical reading, with many exercises for practice in prose and poetry. The exercises are varied in style and carefully fitted to teaching in schools of every grade. In the preface Sanders explains the design of the Fourth Reader. It is made to pass the pupil from the easier ground of the Third to the harder course of the Union Fifth Reader. That Reader is next higher in the series. The book is carefully graded to that middle position.

In one sense, Sanders argues, the Fourth Reader is the most important in the set. The great mass of pupils in common schools are drawn away from school pursuits long before the proper time for a more advanced course. That fact weighed fully in preparing the pages.
snowflakes-and-sunbeams-or-the-young-fur: R. M. Ballantyne wrote The Young Fur-Traders, and the contents open in the middle of an Arctic winter in the wilds of North America. Heads bring in the old fur-trader, who tries to fix his son's flint and finds the task hard, then a counting-room scene. A wolf-hunt on the prairies follows, where Charley stuns his father and breaks in the new horse. Peter Mactavish turns amateur doctor, and Charley airs his views to Kate before the spring brigade sets out.
studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-volume-:
Volume V of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, dated 1927, holds Erotic Symbolism, The Mechanism of Detumescence, and The Psychic State in Pregnancy. Ellis calls these the terminal phenomena of the sexual process, treated before the final volume turns to morals and social hygiene.

Under erotic symbolism Ellis places nearly all the stray forms of the sexual instinct. In each, he argues, some object or act has gained a dynamic power over the mind and body: clear in shoe fetishism, dimmer in exhibitionism. Calling them sexual equivalents only labels them; symbolism, he claims, gives the key that makes them intelligible, whether their roots are inborn, acquired, or both.
ten-reasons-proposed-to-his-adversaries-:
Edmund Campion, a priest of the Society of Jesus, wrote Ten Reasons, his Decem Rationes, as a challenge to foes of the Catholic faith at the English universities. An opening essay in this printing traces the work's long life and high praise.

The essay notes forty-seven printings across Europe and a verdict by Mark Anthony Muret that it was written by the finger of God. It calls the work Campion's last free word on his brief English mission. He had checked the tide of the new faith when the old church seemed down for good. Readers get a famed piece of Elizabethan religious debate, framed by its martyr's fate.
the-abolition-of-slavery-the-right-of-th:
William Lloyd Garrison and others stand behind The Abolition of Slavery. Its full title claims the right of the government under the war power. The pieces argue that the federal war power can end slavery. A part on freedom under the war power opens the book.

That part quotes John Quincy Adams at length. Adams spoke in the House on April 14 and 15, 1842. The topic was war with Great Britain and Mexico. Adams grants that Congress may not meddle with slavery in the states. That holds while slave states keep to their own bounds. But the case changes once the topic is forced on the House. It changes once a member is censured unheard. Readers get a core legal case for wartime freedom. It was built from speeches made years before the Civil War.
the-authoritative-life-of-general-willia:
G. S. Railton, described as first commissioner to General Booth, wrote an authorised life of William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army. Booth was born on April 10, 1829, and died on August 20, 1912, the year this life was copyrighted. A preface by General Bramwell Booth opens the volume.

Twenty-eight chapters trace Booth from childhood and poverty through youth, lay work, and early ministry. Later chapters follow work in East London, the making of an army, and growth in America, Australasia, India, South Africa, and Japan. Final sections cover social work, finance, old age, tributes, organisation, and Booth as a writer.
the-circus-boys-on-the-flying-rings-or-m:
Edgar B. P. Darlington opens this boys' circus tale, subtitled Making the Start in the Sawdust Life, with two boys before a circus billboard. Teddy boasts that he can do what the pictured performer is doing in the air. Phil, his friend, laughs the claim down and corrects his terms.

That is no cartwheel, Phil tells him, but a double somersault, and a real stunt at that. The contents then follow Phil's path: he hears his dismissal, makes his start in the world, and proves his mettle when the circus comes to town. He makes friends with the elephants, enters the sawdust arena, and wins his first call and a thrilling rescue. Setbacks follow, including being left behind and a startling discovery. Darlington gives young readers a backstage path into circus work, from first longing to a solved mystery.
the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bierce-vo: Volume VIII of Ambrose Bierce's collected works gathers his Negligible Tales, On with the Dance, and his Epigrams, shown here in a Gordian Press reprint of 1966. The title page notes that the volume was originally published in 1911. Only the front matter is present here, including the publisher's imprint and Library of Congress card number.A title page and a contents list are all that stand here.
the-continental-monthly-vol-iii-issue-vi:
June 1863 brings the sixth number of volume III of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece is the second part of The Value of the Union. Having surveyed the Union's worth and growth in the first part, the writer now turns to face the pro-slavery rebellion and its drift.

The argument runs through sacred history: a kind Providence, the essay says, has always pushed mankind toward a higher, more united, and happier life, against the drag of selfishness and ignorance. Ages of political upheaval and such religious light as men could take in raised Europe to its state of two and a half centuries ago. There the seeds of religious and political liberty sprouted and crossed to the new world, where they grew into the republic.
the-divine-right-of-church-government-wh: The Divine Right of Church Government argues that rule by preaching and ruling elders alone can claim God's warrant from Scripture. The title page credits sundry ministers of Christ in London. It notes a new, corrected edition printed in New York in 1844. An added part draws on strong writers about church rule. Only the title pages are present here. Their lines cover who may preach, who may join a church, and the people's right to choose pastors.
the-golden-treasury-of-the-best-songs-an: Francis Turner Palgrave selected The Golden Treasury of the Best Songs and Lyrical Pieces in the English Language. Collins' Clear-Type Press printed it in London and Glasgow. Pictures are by A. Pearse. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and Palgrave's dedication to Alfred Tennyson, Poet Laureate. In it he says the book grew under Tennyson's advice. He had hoped to dedicate it to Henry Hallam, who died before it was done. He calls it a true national anthology of three centuries.
the-great-lone-land-a-narrative-of-trave:
Colonel W. F. Butler wrote The Great Lone Land. It is a narrative of travel and adventure in the North-West of America. Sampson Low, Marston and Company printed it in London. It was first published in 1872. The title page quotes Tennyson on a full-fed river and an endless plain. His preface tells of a man at York Factory on Hudson Bay. That man had one fixed resolution. It was to write a book.

The man used to say he would set down all he had seen, and all he had not seen. Butler doubts the plan. People, he says, more readily believe what a man has not seen. He tells of Karkakonias, a Chippeway chief taken to Washington during the Southern War. The aim was to astonish him with American power. He came home silent, and spent his days in smoking and quiet thought.
the-heavenly-footman-or-a-description-of:
John Bunyan wrote The Heavenly Footman, subtitled a description of the man that gets to heaven, with directions how to run so as to obtain. The title page carries the text from First Corinthians: so run, that ye may obtain. An author's letter addresses slothful and careless people at length.

Bunyan warns that sloth in the work of salvation fills the heart with sin, shuts out Christ, and shames the soul. He cites Solomon on the sluggard, the ant as a teacher, and the man who will not plow because of the cold. Neglect of the season for getting heaven, he argues, brings late and bitter repentance in its train.
the-history-of-tom-thumb-to-which-are-ad:
The History of Tom Thumb was edited by Henry Altemus. Two more stories are added to the title tale. They are The Cat and the Mouse and Fire! Fire! Burn Stick! The title story opens in the days of Prince Arthur, king of Britain in the year 516. Merlin, a great magician, travels in beggar's disguise.

Tired, Merlin stops at the cottage of an honest ploughman. The ploughman's wife serves milk and coarse brown bread. Sadness in the neat home leads Merlin to ask its cause. The pair long for a child, he learns. The wife would accept a son no bigger than a thumb. A sibling record tells the same tale with a different opening.
the-inns-and-taverns-of-pickwick-with-so: B. W. Matz wrote this guide to the inns of Dickens's Pickwick Papers, with observations on their other associations. Only the title page and contents are present here. The tour itself does not appear. The contents open with Pickwick and the coaching age. The Golden Cross at Charing Cross comes first. The Bull at Rochester and the White Hart in the Borough follow. Later stops include the Leather Bottle at Cobham, the Great White Horse at Ipswich, and the George and Vulture. A frontispiece shows Pickwick starting for Ipswich.
the-nibelungenlied-translated-into-rhyme:
George Henry Needler's translation of the Nibelungenlied renders the German epic into rhymed English verse in the metre of the original. Needler taught German as associate professor in University College, Toronto. He states his purpose plainly in a preface dated September 1904. He wanted to put a great epic poem, one of the world's finest, within reach of English readers.

Translations are poor substitutes, he concedes, and a new one implies criticism of its predecessors. His apology is that no earlier version reproduced the original's metrical form. His introduction supplies the historical background, summing up research into the saga's origin and growth. Needler had begun the translation years before, while studying the original under Zarncke at Leipzig. Contents outline the introduction's treatment of the saga in its northern and German forms.
the-nile-tributaries-of-abyssinia-and-th:
Only the Project Gutenberg header for The Nile Tributaries of Abyssinia is present here, so Samuel W. Baker's narrative itself does not appear. the-north-pole-its-discovery-in-1909-und:
Robert E. Peary wrote the account of reaching the North Pole in 1909, first published in 1910. Theodore Roosevelt wrote the introduction, and Gilbert H. Grosvenor of the National Geographic Society wrote the foreword. The trip was made under the Peary Arctic Club. Peary dedicated the book to his wife.

An early picture shows five flags planted at the Pole, held by Peary's Inuit companions and Matthew Henson. The flags stand for the Navy League, a college fraternity, the D.A.R. peace cause, and the Red Cross, plus a polar flag Peary had carried for fifteen years. Readers get the commander's own record of the dash to the Pole.
the-outdoor-chums-after-big-game-or-peri: Captain Quincy Allen wrote The Outdoor Chums After Big Game, or Perilous Adventures in the Wilderness, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and a list of the series are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The frontispiece caption shows a beast filled with mad rage galloping straight toward the boys. The series list names companion volumes on the lake, in the forest, and on the Gulf, each at 50 cents postpaid.
the-pony-rider-boys-in-new-mexico-or-the:
Frank Gee Patchin's The Pony Rider Boys in New Mexico, or The End of the Silver Trail, dated 1910, opens aboard an Atlantic and Pacific train. Two men talk in low voices a few seats ahead of four sleeping boys, taking care not to be understood. One has heard of the boys over in Nevada. There are four of them, the Pony Rider Boys, and no tenderfeet, if the stories of their stunts are true.

The talk turns to the stock car up ahead, jammed with stock and equipment. It turns to one slick roan pony a man would not mind owning, by trade or otherwise. A loud snore from Stacy Brown makes both men laugh. Tad Butler rests beside him, and Ned Rector and the fourth boy sleep further back. Patchin lets the reader hear the plotting first, so the danger hangs over the holiday from the opening pages.
the-poor-scholar-traits-and-stories-of-t:
William Carleton's The Poor Scholar stands as Part VI of his Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry. One day about the middle of November, Dominick M'Evoy and his son Jemmy are at work on their potatoes. Their plot lies on Esker Dhu, a hard and barren hill. The day is bitter, the men thinly clad. Sleet-like rain pelts into their garments as the blast sweeps across the hill.

The father, past middle age, holds his miserable farm at a rack-rent and must work it whatever the weather. Pausing on his spade, he looks down at the sheltered inland below. It is inhabited chiefly by Protestants and Presbyterians. He nearly curses them for sitting warm in his people's old possessions. The two ridges before him hold only a poor string of potatoes, one here and one there. Yet the whole ridge must be turned for them.
the-positive-school-of-criminology-three:
Enrico Ferri's The Positive School of Criminology collects three lectures given at the University of Naples on April 22, 23, and 24, 1901. Ernest Untermann translated them, and Charles H. Kerr and Company published them at Chicago in 1908. Untermann's name is printed on this record's own title page. Several hundred students had invited Ferri to sum up the principal conclusions of criminal sociology in short special lectures. He says he gladly accepted.

Two ideals moved him. The first was personal: to spread the scientific ideas his brain had gathered, a prize he credits to his mother's inheritance in the lottery of life. The second was the ideal of young Italy, united in moral and intellectual aims and lifted above the grasp of selfish interests. Without an ideal, Ferri tells his audience, neither an individual nor a whole people can live. It is the fire that makes each life possible, useful, and fertile.
the-power-of-faith-exemplified-in-the-li: The Power of Faith presents the life and writings of the late Mrs. Isabella Graham in a new edition from the American Tract Society. Joanna Bethune entered the copyright in 1843. The edition is enriched by Graham's own narrative of her husband's death and other select correspondence. What appears here is the title page and the start of a detailed contents list. Chapter I covers her early life and residence in Canada, from birth and conversion through marriage to a voyage to Quebec, Montreal, and Antigua, across 1742 to 1772.
the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-in-nine: Volume three of Johnson's works in the nine-volume 1825 edition is shown through title pages and a contents list. A clash stands on those pages: the volume is the third of the set, yet its heading names The Rambler, volume two, and the contents list covers that second Rambler volume. Listed essays run from number 106 to 118. Topics include authors' expectations, prostitutes' misery, and Hymenaeus's courtship. The essays themselves do not appear in the pages present.

Volume four of Johnson's works, in the nine-volume 1825 edition, pairs The Adventurer with The Idler. A prefatory notice explains how The Adventurer began. Dr. John Hawkesworth projected the paper in 1752, admiring The Rambler. Its first number appeared on November 7 that year. Size, price, and publication days matched The Rambler's pattern.

Johnson joined the writers in 1753. His first paper is dated March 3. He then recruited his friend Dr. Joseph Warton to help. Dr. Bathurst, Colman, and Mrs. Chapone also contributed. The notice sets up Johnson's share in a famous periodical. Readers learn how essay papers were planned, staffed, and sustained.
thoughts-i-met-on-the-highway-words-of-f: Ralph Waldo Trine published Thoughts I Met on the Highway with Dodd, Mead in New York in 1919, copyrighted in 1912. The subtitle promises words of friendly cheer from his Life Books. Other Trine titles listed include In Tune with the Infinite and The Land of Living Men. A first line begins by calling thoughts forces that build and attract their like, then breaks off. The title pages and book lists are what is included in this record, so Trine's reflections themselves do not appear beyond that opening line.
timothy-s-quest-a-story-for-anybody-youn: Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote Timothy's Quest, subtitled a story for anybody, young or old, who cares to read it. Houghton, Mifflin published it at Boston and New York, printed at the Riverside Press in Cambridge. A publisher's list prices her Birds' Christmas Carol and Story of Patsy alongside it. Wiggin is also credited with A Summer in a Canon, Children's Rights, and Polly Oliver's Problem in that list. The publisher's catalogue and title page are what is on these pages, so Wiggin's story itself does not appear.
un-doc-agreement-relating-to-the-impleme:
The Agreement on the Implementation of Part XI of the Law of the Sea Convention was signed at New York on 28 July 1994. Part XI governs mining of the deep seabed beyond any state's waters. Rich states had shunned the 1982 pact over those rules. Talks from 1990 to 1994 sought a fix all could accept.

The deal reads Part XI through a market lens. Where the two texts clash, this one wins. Joining the sea pact after 1994 counts as joining this deal too. The deep seabed and its wealth stay the shared birthright of all mankind. The change cleared the way for near-universal buy-in to the sea rules.
un-un-res-agreement-relating-to-the-impl:
Deep seabed mining rules in the Law of the Sea Convention were rewritten by this agreement, adopted by the United Nations in 1994. Part XI of the 1982 convention had set up a strict shared system for mining the ocean floor. Rich states refused to join while those rules stood, and the whole treaty stalled.

The agreement softens the mining rules, cuts costs, and gives market states more say. In exchange, the rest of the convention could enter into force at last. The text is a case study in how a grand treaty gets saved by a practical rewrite.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: A Project Gutenberg header is all that is present here, and Widger's quotations from William Dean Howells are not shown. The header marks the set DW number 04 in the Quotations series by David Widger. It uses the older Gutenberg welcome form, with a state-by-state donation list from about 2000. Readers are told to check the copyright laws of their own country before sharing the file. No title block with release date appears in the portion shown here.
women-in-the-fine-arts-from-the-seventh-: Clara Erskine Clement surveyed women artists from the seventh century B. C. to the twentieth century in this 1904 volume. Pages present here hold her prefatory note and a list of illustrations, but no artist entries. Clement explains that she wrote to artists in Britain, Europe, and America asking about training, honours, and main works. Many sent photographs of their art for the plates. The frontispiece shows Elisabetta Sirani's Infant Christ in Bologna.
wonders-of-creation-a-descriptive-accoun:
Published in 1872 for young readers, this volume describes volcanoes and what they do. Its preface says plain treatment comes first. Hard science and deep theory are left aside on purpose. The hope is that early wonder will push some readers toward later study. A holiday trip to Vesuvius or Etna now sits within reach, the preface notes.

Hecla and its geysers, Cotopaxi, and Kilauea all get named as future goals. The preface also frames volcanoes as proof of divine power and wise limits. Young readers learn basic facts about eruptions, craters, and lava. A sense of awe runs through the lessons.
yorkshire-lyrics-poems-written-in-the-di: John Hartley wrote these lyrics in the dialect spoken in Yorkshire's West Riding. He dedicated the gathering to his daughter Annie Sophie at Christmas 1898. Pages present here hold the title page, that dedication, and a contents list. Titles include Mi Bonny Yorksher Lass, A Tale for th' Childer on Christmas Eve, and Words ov Kindness. A selection of plainer fugitive verses was added, per the title page. The poems themselves do not appear in these pages.
